extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funding (schools, colleges, universities), Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel, and policymakers implementing Title IX grievance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for institutional Title IX grievance procedures about which standard of evidence may be applied, how it must be applied, and related procedural protections to ensure fair, reliable outcomes in sexual harassment matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of Evidence Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have the choice of either applying the preponderance of the evidence standard or the clear and convincing evidence standard when resolving formal complaints of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations revised §106.45(b)(7)(i) to permit recipients to select either standard; the Department believes either may be applied fairly to reach reliable outcomes. Selection represents the degree of confidence decision-makers should have in determinations regarding responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Application of Chosen Standard to All Formal Complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must make its chosen standard of evidence applicable to all formal complaints of sexual harassment, including complaints against employees and faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(1)(vii) requires the choice to be applied consistently to all formal complaints; the Department removed NPRM language that would have limited preponderance to cases with similar maximum sanctions for non-sexual misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted Range of Standards (No Lower/No Higher)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicable standard must not be lower than the preponderance of the evidence standard nor higher than the clear and convincing evidence standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects adoption of standards lower than preponderance (e.g., substantial evidence, reasonable cause, probable cause) and higher than clear and convincing (e.g., beyond a reasonable doubt) because such standards would not yield reliable, fair outcomes in Title IX grievance processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof on the Recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of the applicable evidentiary standard, the burden of proof rests on the recipient, not on either party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients bear responsibility to gather evidence and carry the burden of proof in the grievance process; parties have rights to participate, but the institutional burden remains central to fairness and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Evaluation and Prohibition on Status-Based Credibility Determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers must assess credibility based on objective evaluation of the evidence and not on a party's status as a complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must avoid prejudgment or bias for or against complainants or respondents generally or an individual party; credibility should not be presumed because of role (e.g., faculty vs. student).

rubrics_metrics.name: No Corroboration Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the preponderance of the evidence standard nor the clear and convincing evidence standard requires corroborating evidence to reach a determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies that determinations can be based solely on the parties' statements when appropriate; decision-makers must objectively evaluate all relevant evidence, inculpatory and exculpatory, and may reach conclusions without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance Notice of Institutional Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must notify students and employees in advance of the standard of evidence they will apply in sexual harassment grievance processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance notification increases predictability and transparency so affected parties understand the 'degree of confidence' required for determinations under the recipient's process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Defines Degree of Confidence, Not Required Evidence Types
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard of evidence represents the degree of confidence a decision-maker must have in the correctness of factual conclusions; it does not dictate the type or nature of evidence that must be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of standard does not mandate particular forms of proof; decision-makers consider the persuasiveness/weight of available evidence to reach the required level of confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Protections and Party Participation Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.45, parties have explicit procedural rights: to gather, present, review, and respond to evidence; to review the investigative report; to pose questions to be answered by a respondent; and to have an advisor of choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural features, paired with the chosen standard of evidence, are intended to produce consistent, fair, and reliable outcomes without transforming campuses into de facto civil courts (no full civil discovery or motion practice required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive Measures and Remedies Independent of Grievance Outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainants may receive supportive measures when sexual harassment is reported, regardless of whether a formal complaint is filed; recipients may continue supportive measures even after a determination of not responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must offer supportive measures upon notice of harassment; §106.71 also cautions recipients not to draw conclusions about truthfulness based solely on case outcomes. Remedies to restore equal access are required for complainants where fair processes reach accurate determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Using Outcome Alone as Basis for Bad-Faith Findings
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not rely solely on the outcome of a grievance process to conclude that a party made a bad-faith, materially false statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.71 prohibits basing bad-faith materially false statement findings solely on case outcome; recipients may sanction bad-faith false statements but must have independent basis beyond the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection Should Promote Accurate, Reliable Outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should select the standard of evidence they reasonably believe will, together with required procedural protections, produce accurate determinations regarding responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes research is inconclusive about which standard minimizes false positives vs. false negatives; the key is combining an appropriate standard with the §106.45 protections to minimize erroneous outcomes and ensure fairness to both complainants and respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional Due Process and Fundamental Fairness Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the preponderance of the evidence standard or the clear and convincing standard is consistent with constitutional due process and fundamental fairness in Title IX grievance processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department is not aware of federal appellate precedent requiring one standard over the other in Title IX contexts; recipients must still design processes that satisfy due process protections appropriate to the institutional setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted Institutional Flexibility and National Variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations permit recipients to choose between the two permitted standards, which may result in different standards across institutions; the Department does not consider such variation to constitute unequal justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The approach preserves recipient discretion while requiring transparency and consistent application within an institution; Clery Act reporting obligations are not altered by a recipient's choice of evidentiary standard.
